lesson.title: Differentiating Any Polynomial, Term by Term
lesson.summary: Combining the power rule with linearity lets you differentiate any polynomial by applying the power rule to each term and adding the results, with no limit computation required.
lesson.body:
A polynomial is a sum of constant multiples of powers of x, such as a_n x^n plus a_(n-1) x^(n-1), continuing down to a constant term a_0. Every single piece of that description matches exactly the tools built in the previous chapters: powers of x are handled by the power rule, constant multiples are handled by the constant multiple rule, and the sum holding everything together is handled by linearity, which is the sum and constant multiple rules working in combination. Put together, this means any polynomial can be differentiated term by term, applying the power rule to each power of x, without ever setting up a limit directly on the full polynomial.

In general, if p(x) = a_n x^n + a_(n-1) x^(n-1) + ... + a_1 x + a_0, then p'(x) = n a_n x^(n-1) + (n-1) a_(n-1) x^(n-2) + ... + a_1, and the constant term a_0 simply disappears, since its derivative is 0 by the constant rule. Notice that a polynomial of degree n produces a derivative that is a polynomial of degree n-1, one degree lower, which matches what happens in every earlier example: x^3 became 3x^2, and x^2 became 2x.

Here is a full worked example, checked two different ways. Let p(x) = x^3 - 2x^2 + 4x - 1. Differentiating term by term: the derivative of x^3 is 3x^2, the derivative of -2x^2 is -2 times 2x, which is -4x, the derivative of 4x is 4, and the derivative of -1 is 0. Adding these gives p'(x) = 3x^2 - 4x + 4. At x = 2, this evaluates to p'(2) = 3(4) - 4(2) + 4 = 12 - 8 + 4 = 8.

To double check this answer numerically, compare it against a very small difference quotient directly on p, using h = 0.001. First, p(2) = 8 - 2(4) + 4(2) - 1 = 8 - 8 + 8 - 1 = 7. Next, p(2.001) requires (2.001)^3 = 8.012006001, so -2(2.001)^2 = -2(4.004001) = -8.008002, and 4(2.001) = 8.004. Adding everything: 8.012006001 - 8.008002 + 8.004 - 1 = 7.008004001. The difference quotient is [p(2.001) - p(2)] / 0.001 = (7.008004001 - 7) / 0.001 = 0.008004001 / 0.001 = 8.004001. This numerical estimate, 8.004, lands extremely close to the exact derivative value of 8 found above, with the small remaining gap explained by h not being infinitesimally small, exactly as the limit definition predicts.

This term by term method works for a polynomial of any degree, with any number of terms, positive or negative coefficients included. It is the direct payoff of every rule proven in this sequence of chapters: what would have required an increasingly painful binomial expansion inside a single limit, term by term for a high degree polynomial, now reduces to reading off exponents and multiplying, one clean step at a time.

It is also worth noticing the pattern in what disappears and what survives. The constant term always vanishes, since it has no x attached, consistent with the constant rule. Every other term loses exactly one degree, since the power rule always subtracts 1 from the exponent it acts on. A degree 3 polynomial like the example above therefore always produces a degree 2 derivative, a degree 4 polynomial produces a degree 3 derivative, and so on, which gives a quick sanity check: if your computed derivative does not have degree exactly one less than the original polynomial, a term by term differentiation step was likely skipped or miscalculated somewhere along the way.
